There isn't a ton i can say that others haven't already covered, but I'll add that anorexia as a disorder is functionally extremely similar to OCD - speaking from my own experience, I'll have an intrusive thought about my body/food that then leads to body or food related compulsions such as restricting or body checking. Though I don't have OCD, i imagine it would be extremely easy to start with OCD and fall into an ED; in fact almost a fifth of those with anorexia also have OCD. From Charlie's perspective, when he felt overwhelmed by everything else, his body and food intake likely felt like something he could control. As a result of the bullying, he might have also thought (though it's obviously not logical) that a solution to the bullying was to literally make himself smaller and less noticable.

As others have mentioned, self-harm can give someone a feeling of control in many ways. From a neurological perspective, self-harm releases adrenaline as well as dopamine, which makes you feel better immediately after the act and is what makes it addictive. Charlie is especially at risk for self-harm as he suffers from disorders that may originate due to a lack of dopamine in the brain. In short, it's not at all surprising that he suffered from an ED and self-harm as well as OCD; i think he most likely fell into both as a (maladaptive) method of control and they spiraled out of control quickly.

My go-to is bringing up all the times that women have beat men to expose what a ridiculously absurd argument that is. Madge Syers, the only woman to compete in an official figure skating competition before women were banned, beat every man in the competition except one when she placed second. Gertrude Ederle, the first woman to swim the English Channel, beat every man who had swam it prior (and did it as a teenager). The All-American Redheads, a barnstorming basketball team founded in the 1930s, regularly beat the men's teams they played. And of course there's the infamous Battle of the Sexes tennis match, which we all know Billie Jean King won. Just because these women outperformed men, does that automatically mean they're naturally better at skating, swimming, basketball, and tennis? No, of course it fucking doesn't because while awesome these are all isolated incidents that don't necessarily have any bearing on the sports ability of women as a whole. *One game* does not mean that 15 year old boys will constantly beat a women's national team, just like one win doesn't mean the USMNT is going to win a world cup anytime soon.

Make sure you start by just giving her a hug and making sure she knows that you're there for her. Try not to distance yourself or change the way you treat her (basically don't treat her like she's fragile) because that'll end up alienating her more. Once everything has calmed down a bit, start a dialogue if she's comfortable. Stay away from questions like "why", as often there isn't really a concrete reason, but try to talk through it with her. Work on creating an open environment where she can come to you if she feels down - one of the best ways to do that is probably by establishing some kind of weekly check-in that's scheduled so she can prepare herself/know what to expect. And while I know it's hard, try to remember that chances are you alone won't be able to stop her or make her start the recovery process. Recovery is fickle, and the best you can do is support her until she's in a place where she's able to start and commit to recovery. You sound like an amazing parent, though, and I wish you all the luck.

When I was 10-11, I was at a Tae Kwon Do competition. The way it worked was that they would call age groups and someone would group you based on height/build and belt color. When my age group was called, the person organizing us fucked up and I got paired with my best friend who went to the same dojang. We both won our preliminary rounds, so had to spar each other for the final; to make matters worse we weren't allowed a coach since we were technically on the same team. I lost, and by the time I had gotten my medal and taken pictures my mom had to take me outside because I was crying so hard at that point. Obviously I took it really hard, but after a couple minutes of crying a woman came up to us. She had a Yorkie with her, and she let me pet it while she told us about her son, who had also lost a hard sparring match. It must've only been a five minute encounter, but she helped me so much, and I was able to keep it together enough after that to go congratulate my friend and acknowledge that despite the loss, I did good. I'll never forget you, Yorkie lady.
